items.question: Why do you see robots being able to manufacture themselves as a potential milestone in robotics?
items.object: Robots assembling and manufacturing themselves
items.answer: What I’ve always really wanted is for robots to be able to make themselves. I think robots being able to assemble and make themselves is a manifestation of reproduction.

items.question: What do you think robotics research and writing fiction have in common?
items.object: Creativity and execution in robotics research and fiction writing
items.answer: I think both require some creativity. For example, if a robot still does many tasks poorly, you need to come up with new methods. With fiction, perhaps the story you truly want to write has not yet been written, so you need to create it. Often that takes fairly unconstrained, imaginative ideas. They also require execution. In research, after I have an idea, I gradually put it into practice, which involves engineering work—coding, for example. Writing fiction can begin with a premise, and then, to make readers feel that premise, you start typing it out word by word.

items.question: What especially fascinates you about science fiction?
items.object: Science fiction’s exploration of productivity and human relationships
items.answer: I mostly write science fiction, which is also one of my favorite categories to read. I think science fiction certainly relates to Silicon Valley and the era we are living in. Two themes in science fiction especially fascinate me. First: after productivity changes, how do people’s lives change? Second: in a futuristic, science-fiction society very unlike our social landscape, what are relationships between people like? The first theme is probably more connected to my work. At work, we often consider that AI research and robotics are forms of automation: after automating many things people currently do and improving efficiency, what will people do? That is a question I think about every day.

items.question: How has building a general-purpose robot brain changed your understanding of team collaboration?
items.object: Team collaboration in building a general-purpose robot brain
items.answer: After graduating from my PhD, I joined this startup making embodied-intelligence brains for robots. items.question: How do you imagine personal bots changing the way people navigate an era of information explosion?
items.object: Personal bots as intermediaries for navigating internet information
items.answer: I get inspiration from that relationship when conceiving fiction. One idea is that we are now in an era of information explosion. I think some people may already be like this. items.question: How do you understand the current limits of AI agents?
items.object: The current limits of AI agents
items.answer: The permissions agents receive, the responsibilities they bear, and what they can do are all relatively limited. With permissions, people often prompt them: if you are unsure, do not rush to act; confirm with a person first. As for responsibility: I injured myself while rock climbing and sought medical advice everywhere. Healthcare in the United States can be difficult, so I would give some medical information to an agent and ask it to explain. But I would never fully trust its answer; I cannot simply believe whatever AI tells me, right? I would still take it to a human expert for confirmation. I do not think it can bear responsibility if I act on its recommendation. In human society, trust is built by whoever can bear responsibility. That trust is still evolving; we have not reached the point of completely trusting an agent and giving it so much authority. Finally, what it can do remains limited. In robotics we sometimes joke—perhaps this joke is already outdated—that three or four years ago, talking to a fellow student close to graduating, we complained: what do we do every day? We make a robot put a red block on a blue block. Isn’t that something a three-year-old can do? We spend five years getting PhDs teaching robots to do it, perhaps not even as well as a three-year-old.

items.question: How do you see the role informatics competitions played in shaping your life?
items.object: The role of informatics competitions in shaping Kay Ke’s life
items.answer: I think there have been key turning points in my life, all influenced to some degree by my participation in informatics competitions. I was born in Anhui Province and went to school in Wuhu, Anhui. Objectively, its educational resources may lag behind big cities such as Shanghai. But by coincidence, our city had an outstanding informatics-competition teacher. When he was a student in our city, he was injured in an accident and lost both hands. That experience may have affected his employment choices, leading him to return to his hometown. He became a computer teacher. He was extremely smart and outstanding, and devoted himself to computer education. His name was Jiang Tao. I never actually spoke with him face to face, but I benefited from many of his contributions. He established a systematic, tiered training program for competitions in our city. Like the Olympic-math classes we took as children, our city had formal informatics Olympiad classes as extracurricular interest classes. I started learning it at eight. As children, we did not think much about it; we just thought we could play on computers and were thrilled. As long as I did not have to study something serious and could play with something less serious, I was very happy. In that process, I inadvertently laid the groundwork for later programming and gradually entered the competition path. As I grew up, I explored other careers too. I actually studied psychology in college, then switched to economics.

items.question: How do you think about fairness in access to educational resources?
items.object: Fairness in access to educational resources
items.answer: There really are not so many things in life that are absolutely fair; even the definition of fairness is vague. Different people may think differently. I only try to preserve a kind of fairness within my own abilities. Often, no one has the right to demand that another person act according to their own ideas. But above that, there are things I think have universal value. One is perhaps educational resources. After going abroad, I had some feelings about it. During my education in China, I once wanted to attend Tsinghua or Peking University and considered taking the exams. But in Anhui, perhaps only three or four out of every ten thousand people can get into those schools. I was in a competition class in high school and followed the conventional academic path step by step. I was not exceptionally outstanding—not someone who truly loved studying to their core and spent enormous time studying. I was middling in the competition class: I studied more of what I liked and less of what I did not. So I knew I could perhaps compete for those three or four spots out of ten thousand only if I changed my nature and worked exceptionally hard. After leaving, I found that some other provinces truly had advantages in educational resources. In big cities, perhaps eighty out of ten thousand can get into Tsinghua or Peking University. In Anhui, one would not even dare imagine such figures. It felt like an issue of resource allocation. But at this point in time, what I think about more is how creating new productivity can, on some level, smooth out those inequities.

items.question: How do you understand game theory’s usefulness across economics and machine learning?
items.object: Game theory’s applications in economics and machine learning
items.answer: Put crudely, game theory often says that if two people are playing a game in an adversarial relationship, both must do the best they can within their scope. But through competing, they may reach an equilibrium. You may guide them so that the equilibrium they reach through competition is optimal. I think that explains many present market-competition relationships in economics: everyone competes intensely in the market, and in the end reaches an equilibrium beneficial to society’s development. That idea also has applications in machine learning. Around 2016, generative adversarial networks appeared. They contain many game-theoretic elements: there is a generator and a judge, playing a game with each other. To use an imperfect analogy, the generator makes counterfeit money, while the judge distinguishes whether a bill is real or fake. Over time the generator is led to produce counterfeit bills increasingly like real ones; when the adversary truly cannot tell them apart, it can only guess. Using this idea, people created image-generation technologies that generated fake images appearing like the real world. Through gradual adversarial competition, the image becomes indistinguishable from a real photo, making generated images look more real. So I think game theory has very broad applications in machine learning, continuing to today—in machine-learning safety and in making machines’ ways of thinking or generating more like humans.

items.question: Why do you find reinforcement learning more appealing than imitation learning in robotics?
items.object: Reinforcement learning versus imitation learning in robotics
items.answer: Within robotics, my research path began with imitation learning and ultimately moved to reinforcement learning. I think that fits my personality somewhat, so now I do more reinforcement learning.

items.question: How did you think about learning robot intelligence directly from data when you were working in a traditional robotics lab in 2017?
items.object: Learning robot intelligence from data versus traditional planning and control
items.answer: The lab and advisor I joined were more in the traditional camp. Robotics had already developed for decades and had many successful applications. People joke that we have sent rockets into space and can explore Mars; those all use much robotics technology. Around 2017, the traditional camp focused more on path planning—and control problems. This accords with human intuition: to do something, first plan step one, two, and three, connect them into a full plan, then use control to execute it gradually, ensuring that each step is done correctly and appropriately. Since I started from machine learning, I wondered in 2017: many fields can learn from data, so could a robot’s intelligence also come directly from data, rather than rules I set? This idea was rather niche compared with the traditional methods in my lab. I was the only one there doing something similar.

items.question: What draws you to data-driven machine learning as a way of solving problems?
items.object: Data-driven machine learning and black-box optimization
items.answer: This is actually a little interesting. I think it is a subtle state of knowing that something works without knowing why it works. For some problems, people want to get to the bottom of things. But in optimization, everyone wants to optimize; I think there is a part of one’s personality that wants things better and stronger. One class is black-box optimization: do not care or ask how it works; it gives a very good solution. As long as you know how to design a system that can provide a relatively good solution, you do not need to know how it operates in the end. This was also a major debate in NLP around 2016–17. Traditional NLP used semantics and structure, methods closer to how humans understand language: divide semantics into many parts, requiring many experts to understand and learn them, then automate and feed them to machines. Data-driven methods were not entirely unaffected by previous work, but their way of operating changed completely: learn directly from data, omit the intermediate steps, become end-to-end. I think robotics may need to follow a similar path.

items.question: How do you see Carnegie Mellon University's role in the history of robotics?
items.object: Carnegie Mellon University's role in the history of robotics
items.answer: My perspective may be incomplete, but I will try to recount it. I will talk about some representative researchers I have encountered or felt connected to. I think the history of robotics cannot avoid developments at Carnegie Mellon University. Carnegie Mellon has its own Robotics Institute, established around 1979 or in the 1980s, so it has now existed for more than forty years. They began researching how robots could perceive and see, make decisions, and move. I think this combination of seeing and moving began with them and gradually became very popular. They developed many branches: after enabling robots to make decisions, putting them in real environments for disaster relief; and autonomous driving around 2000. CMU made a major splash in that area, and people suddenly felt autonomous driving could begin. The 2004 and 2005 DARPA autonomous-driving competitions stimulated the founding of many autonomous-driving companies around 2006, which I think was very motivating. Later, perhaps most relevant to us, CMU developed machine-learning scholars, manipulation scholars—manipulation means using hands or robot hands to do things—and people studying how machines and humans coexist in life. Among these, manipulation is perhaps more representative, because its founder is in my academic lineage, so I know more about it.

items.answer: It is fundamentally a preference for different ways of solving problems. items.question: Why do you favor machine learning over relying solely on traditional methods in robotics?
items.object: Machine-learning methods versus traditional methods in robotics
items.answer: I think it is practicality, and also a kind of faith: how to make it happen. At the present moment, I want to choose the method I think is most likely to make it happen. I do not really believe traditional methods alone are enough. I think we can all benefit from traditional methods, but I do not think using them alone is sufficient. There is fairly broad consensus on this. If you abstract every problem as an input-output curve, traditional methods give a clear curve: put in a certain amount and the output is relatively clear. When Boston Dynamics made its backflip, for example, it was incredibly, incredibly impressive; no one had dared to do it or even imagine it. But they did it at the cost of many engineers constantly tuning parameters and adapting them to the task and desired result. If you do a new task, you still need that much investment. With machine-learning algorithms, first, we do not need engineers to do it, right? Through all kinds of setups, we let the algorithm do it itself. Your workload as an engineer becomes smaller. For instance, many cool parkour videos today probably require an amount of work incomparable to that era. Second, once something requires less human labor, interaction changes too: how can ordinary people interact with it? With today's AI agents, perhaps initially they were fairly niche—you had to be an expert and know how to use them, because they could be hard to use. Robotics is somewhat in that state now: it may run, but you may need an expert to roughly understand its problems and make corrections in advance for it to run better. But I think the overall trend is toward enabling an ordinary person to interact naturally with an agent and get the result they want.

items.question: Why do you think quadruped robots produced more strong results than robotic manipulation under traditional physics-based approaches?
items.object: Physical modeling in robotic manipulation versus quadruped locomotion
items.answer: One unavoidable challenge in manipulation is the issue my advisor mentioned: I do not know the friction. Every object can have different friction—this microphone, our clothes, their folds—countless things are difficult to model. If you use traditional thinking, you have to model them all. If you do not know what consequences your actions will have, how can you solve the problem? That is a major traditional line of thinking, and one behind algorithms based on physical models. For a dog, contact is more instantaneous: my leg runs on the ground and touches it briefly. Often, you do not need to understand in detail the friction between my leg and the ground. So I think dogs may require less physical knowledge, while manipulation requires more physical knowledge. That is why, relatively speaking, there were fewer very good manipulation results than dog results at the time.

items.question: Why did you see reinforcement learning as the next step after teaching your chopsticks robot to pick up a ball?

items.answer: After that work, I told my advisor it was not enough, because I was still grasping too slowly. After all, I was operating the robot and constantly adjusting my own movements. I was exerting a great deal of effort to provide the robot with very high-quality data so it could learn better. But that was too tiring—how could lazy people do that? We needed to let it explore itself and discover how to surpass the data I provided, so it could do better. Later, the focus shifted to reinforcement learning: letting the robot do this in the real world, practice continuously, and improve through learning from practice. It is a little like watching interviews with Olympic champions and their training to motivate yourself. To do something well, especially something motoric, you really need to adapt and develop a strategy best suited to your body, then continually train your body until you carve out muscle memory. For people, that is muscle memory; for machine learning, I think it is a reinforcement-learning process.

items.question: How do you think about the tension between generalization and performance when choosing problems for machine-learning research?
items.object: The tension between generalization and performance in machine-learning research
items.answer: I think elegance is very subjective. In that era, during my PhD, we went from a relatively emerging branch to an algorithmic approach people were increasingly willing to accept. There were skeptical voices then, and I think their challenges were entirely valid. They asked factual questions such as: if you can do everything but do nothing well, what is this algorithm useful for? I think that was a very meaningful concern at the time. When people make many things, looking forward you do not understand; only looking back may you trace things to representative or contributing work. When deciding what to do next, this idea inspired at least my own research: I wanted machine learning to do at least one problem to the extreme, so that others might find it simpler to generalize it, because they could directly transfer from my experience to other tasks. The conflict between generalization and performance remains the core issue. Even today, I think that challenge has not completely disappeared; even practitioners like us are constantly thinking about it.

items.question: How do you assess the robustness of machine learning compared with traditional methods in industrial robotics?
items.object: Robustness of machine learning compared with traditional industrial robotics
items.answer: Consider a traditional robotics pipeline in a factory: using a large robot arm to put a windshield onto a car. This is a problem traditional methods have solved very maturely, with strong guarantees of success rate, stability, and speed. Compared with traditional methods, no one can yet really say that the algorithms and performance obtained through machine learning have robustness equal to the traditional approach. I think that remains a frontier research problem even today.

items.question: How do you interpret Jitendra’s statement that “Robotics is far too important to be left for robotists” in relation to robot foundation-model development?
items.object: Jitendra’s statement that robotics is too important to be left to roboticists
items.answer: I think this is such a fun quote. There are many interpretations. A less friendly one may be: robotics is too important; these robotics people cannot do it, so we have to step in to make it happen. But I think there is a friendlier interpretation: to make robotics happen, people from different industries must pool their efforts. I think this is instructive for today's robot foundation-model development. For instance, I come from a relatively traditional lineage, so I may focus a great deal on motions, mechanics themselves, and refinement of performance; I also do algorithms. But outside my field there are people in vision who have more experience bringing in and training on more data, and people working on large language models who have more large-model training experience. I think robotics can succeed only by bringing together every walk of life: software algorithms, training from different fields, large models, hardware, and even supply chains.

items.question: How do you understand traditional robotics researchers’ response to the growing role of machine learning in robotics?
items.object: Traditional robotics researchers’ relationship with machine learning
items.answer: I think there are two points. First, many people are actively embracing and exploring it. You originally had one toolkit for doing many things; now others tell you they have another toolkit, a very exciting one. You may not initially agree that it is exciting, but after seeing some things, you may change and say this toolkit might be exciting—how can we explore and experiment with it? You might combine approaches, change directions, or open up a new direction. I think this is happening constantly. On the other hand, traditional-school people have a great deal of expert insight. To do their tasks well, many have gone through extensive hardware transformations and engineering refinement. If they share insights within current projects, I think what they say is very reasonable. For example, last night I was reading a blog about motor issues. The author came from machine learning and was studying motors; at the end, he also thanked many traditional-school professors at CMU for their guidance.

items.question: How do you understand the similarities and differences between Pi and Scale as companies building robot brains?
items.object: Pi and Scale’s approaches to embodied intelligence
items.answer: I can only share what I understand and have encountered. I feel Pi and Scale both have a strong label of academic people starting companies. The founders and co-founders of both were professors, and some were highly productive professors. Their slogans are also somewhat similar: they both want to create a general, embodied-intelligence, foundation-model brain. In terms of differences, Pi thinks more about bimanual manipulation—trying to solve manipulation, because many scholars who joined Pi feel that much good progress has been made in mobility, and now we should think about how to make great progress in picking things up and putting them down. You could make the bold claim that if you solve pick-and-place, you can eliminate all household chores in life. You are just picking up and putting down: pick this thing up, put it there, perhaps with path and trajectory constraints. But it is a broad category of problems worth solving. At Scale, relatively speaking, there is more exploration of humanoids and dogs.

items.question: Why do you describe Google's research organization as the “Whampoa Military Academy” of robotics startups in early 2023?

items.question: How do you understand the differences in how traditional robotics researchers and large-model researchers approach building robots?
items.object: Differences between traditional robotics researchers and large-model researchers
items.answer: I can increasingly feel that to make robots happen, in a team environment we need to absorb everyone's strengths; people from all walks of life need to join in. As for differences, let me put it this way: suppose a robot collects one data point. Large-model people might think, “What if we collect a million such data points?” Then we get a number, and once we have that number, we make it better and better and better. People coming more from traditional robotics might first think: what does this data point look like? I want to inspect its motion, what it did, including the hardware conditions and environment in which it was collected. You can see that machine-learning scholars from traditional robotics care relatively more about physical motion, while scholars from large models often airily say, “The information now seems incomplete; let us add or fill in a piece.” I think that may be because after doing robotics many times, you become accustomed to current robot perception systems, whereas large-model people can more readily step outside that framework and think about what information we need to make this happen.

items.question: How do you think a robot's physical configuration affects its ability to learn complex tasks and transfer them to a humanoid?

items.answer: I think task complexity can be separated into several levels. A humanoid has many joints, so controlling all those joints simultaneously is difficult. Whether you do it with a humanoid or a simpler bimanual robot, you are completing a difficult task. So if I can accomplish a highly complex task with a simple configuration, I think the probability that it can transfer to a humanoid later is also very high.

items.question: How do you think about what makes a robotics research lab a frontier lab?
items.object: The frontier of robotics research and the difficulty of evaluating robot models
items.answer: I think the frontier is everywhere; we still have a long way to go. One thing I feel especially directly is evaluation. I actually think NLP has already gone down this road. Back then, for natural language, they would generate a passage and ask you to score it, and how you score it is not easy either. But on the robotics side, it is even worse: you have to run it on a robot before you can know what it did and score it. Not only is the score somewhat hard to assign, but you are also constrained by mechanics and physics. A lot of the time, there may just be some changes that you yourself do not know about, and they affect your model’s performance. I believe that at the final product stage, you should not be too afraid of these small changes. Or, say, you need to pick up this cup, right? Suppose the task we are doing now is picking up this cup. Putting the cup anywhere on the table is one way to perturb it—seeing whether it can pick it up from every location. You also need to look at different lighting, different backgrounds, the table height, perhaps it is not even a table but a pedestal sticking up; can it pick it up? Or the cup itself may be at an angle. There are endlessly many initial conditions that may all affect final performance. So during evaluation, you hope to assess all these things, but in real life you cannot necessarily control them that well. Evaluation is now a problem, and that directly leads to how we understand the frontier. Unlike other fields, there is something like a leaderboard: hey, we released a huge dataset, every model runs on it, a racetrack, and you can see which horse wins. You can relatively objectively—relatively objectively and clearly—see a definite result for something like that. One reason it is hard to discuss the frontier in robotics is that evaluation is so difficult that it is hard to evaluate it thoroughly. Every company, I believe, has its own internal evaluation system, and what it emphasizes may not be the same as what another company emphasizes. But stepping back, I also think this is temporary. In the end, what gets built should not be too worried about this. Maybe everyone is still exploring how to make things more robust and broad.

items.question: How do you think about the relationship between a robotic arm’s task-level decisions and its low-level control?
items.object: The two-level architecture of robotic arm control
items.answer: Once the arm can be assembled, you need to write systems and drivers for it. At the lowest level, it is all electrical power or pneumatic pressure: you send it some signal, and in response it begins to perform movements. A very ordinary control method is position control: I want this joint to be at a 90-degree angle now and change it to 180 degrees, so I send that command. At the joint level, it needs to convert the signal sent from above into something it can actually execute. That is called low-level control. One layer above that, how do you decide what position signals to send? Very likely you need a brain that sees the current task and decides, oh, to do this task—to pick something up from the table—I first need to lift my hand. It needs to understand the task and understand your joints, then make a decision such as lifting this elbow joint—send it to the mechanical joint, and the joint executes it. After execution there is a new scene. The brain sees the new scene: oh, I am already above the table; the next action may be to go right or left. I think this is a two-level way of thinking: a brain makes decisions and turns them into something understandable and executable, which is also convenient for us to debug. At the same time, something at a lower level translates it into a more primitive thing in the physical world.

items.question: How do you understand the significance of the capabilities demonstrated by Pi 0?
items.object: Pi 0’s demonstration of robotic capabilities
items.answer: I think Pi 0’s keyword should be capability. When Pi 0 first began, I think everyone was very excited: we had a very good architecture and could approach robotics with the mindset of large models, but no one knew what it would turn into or what it could do. Pi was founded in early 2024, and we wanted to do things that could not be done before, but specifically making those previously impossible things happen—that was the journey of Pi 0. Pi 0 did three tasks. The first, which people may be familiar with, was folding clothes. I think the clothes-folding result we published in November 2024 was eye-opening; people had never seen performance on a task at that level before. The second was folding boxes—folding cardboard boxes—which was also a, wow, can this thing really do that? We did not know; let’s try. There was also a third one at the time: bussing, going to a table to grasp, pick up, and place things, but with unprecedented diversity of objects and still handling them all well. These three tasks laid the foundation, I think, for what large models could do on tasks that previously seemed unimaginable, so the emphasis was on performance.

items.question: What do you find intellectually exciting about Pi 0.5’s exploration of generalization across homes?
items.object: Pi 0.5’s exploration of generalization across homes
items.answer: I think the significance of generalization still exists today. After you train a large model, a fundamental machine-learning question is the so-called in-domain versus out-of-domain question: data inside the distribution and outside it. If, after training, it can only perform well within the data distribution and is useless outside it, then its impact is very limited, right? So generalization is emphasized. Suppose you collected data for a task in House A. You put it in House B or House C, or investigate how many houses—100 houses, 1,000 houses—you need to collect data in before you get good results in the 10,001st house. I think Pi 0.5 was born to explore whether our large model could generalize, and under what conditions it could generalize. Meanwhile, there were other publications between Pi 0 and Pi 0.5 that improved the large model’s expressive and hierarchical capabilities, enabling such generalization. At the time, we collected data in many Airbnbs—in other people’s homes. Because we went out into the world, it was not an office scene that we controlled, nor a factory scene controlled by someone else. We really collected data for everyday tasks in messy, unstructured homes belonging to other people, and studied how it would perform in new homes once it had that data. One exciting point was that we collected data from about—I remember the paper said—100 homes, then tried removing homes from that set and seeing how far performance continued to improve. We felt the curve was flattening: perhaps you do not truly need to collect data in every home in the world before working in their homes. There may be some number that, once you reach it, is enough. What is exciting about generalization is that the in-distribution data may have a required size, and reaching that size may perhaps be sufficient.

It can then achieve better results than before, better than with the fixed data you previously collected. I think it has substantial implications for our data collection.

items.question: How do you see robot-generated experience addressing the limits of teleoperated data collection?
items.object: Robot-generated experiential data and the limits of teleoperated data collection
items.answer: Usually, when we collect real-robot data, there is an arm—for example, I put an arm at this table—and then I can use teleoperation to make it do things. The data you collect is a machine fixed to the table doing a task. It does not actually have to be teleoperated; you can let it do the task itself, and then collect all that data—the sources of data can actually be very broad. Previously, many people said that if our robotics field relies on humans for teleoperation, data collection is slow and poor. I think it can be improved further, but that concern does exist: perhaps in the future we cannot collect all the data we want entirely that way. After the Pi 0.6 project, we also felt strongly that data generated by robots themselves can be very powerful. The starting point is set by humans, but to surpass that starting point, robots still have to act in the environment. Personally, I am quite bullish—quite firmly optimistic—that robots in the future should be cheap and convenient. Very likely, many people’s present concerns about data will not matter over the long arc of time, because the data collected by so many robots during deployment can all be put to use for me.

items.question: Why do you think corrective data matters for training robot models?
items.object: Corrective data in robot learning
items.answer: I think that is part of the action, part of the task. This idea was already present a lot in early imitation learning. A very serious problem in imitation learning is accumulated errors: tiny errors at every step may keep amplifying until the robot reaches a terrible situation it never anticipated, one that would not occur in data collected by humans. Once the robot enters that situation, it may not know how to correct its trajectory and complete the task. There is a whole set of technical fixes for this problem. So many people strongly emphasize, when collecting data, that we should collect not only perfect human data, but also lots of corrective data: once a robot reaches a bad situation, how does it recover and continue completing the task? Corrective data is indeed important to the performance of a robot large model. But again, corrective data can also be collected by robots running on their own. That is a fairly essential aspect of reinforcement learning.

items.question: How do you understand the kinds of generalization demonstrated by Pi Zero’s table-clearing and clothes-folding tasks?
items.object: Generalization in Pi Zero’s table-clearing and clothes-folding tasks
items.answer: At the time, generalization during the Pi Zero period was more carried by the table-clearing task. For generalization, we had hundreds of props for table clearing; we could have it clear them at random and swap in all kinds of things, letting the data-collection people use their own imagination to make things up. As for the other two tasks, first, they are generalizable too, because generalization is not a single standard; it has many different details. For folding clothes, clothing has countless states, right? One extra fold here, a bend there—each is a different state. No matter how you collect states, you still have only a finite number, and cannot cover every possible state of clothes. How do you ensure it can still complete the task? You already need some generalization. Then there are different clothes: one is red, another is green. Different clothes are another kind of generalization. Even in the later Pi 0.6* work, folding more clothes meant beginning to fold different categories of garments; that is another dimension of generalization. So I do not think these tasks lack generalization. They just explore different kinds of it. One reason we did not know whether it could do these tasks was that we knew clothes folding might encounter all kinds of situations absent from the data, and we did not know whether it could handle them. Think of it this way: whatever the garment in front of it is, the first step is to touch it. But how do you ensure your model can do that? You still have to go in and see.

items.question: Why do you think throughput is a useful way to evaluate robot performance in Pi 0.6*?

There are also finer-grained aspects: the definition of a task succeeding or failing has been refined by us. When a person does a task, or a robot does one, there are many implicit meanings. items.question: What do you find valuable about Physical Intelligence’s FAST and Hi Robot papers, released between Pi 0 and Pi 0.5?
items.object: Physical Intelligence’s FAST and Hi Robot research
items.answer: I think some of the research in between was also very inspiring. Research is really a continual process of waves crashing over waves—the earlier wave dies on the beach—but if you can make a wave, it is very inspiring and can contribute a lot to the waves that come later. Pi released two works between Pi 0 and Pi 0.5 that I think were very interesting. One was FAST. It studied, from the perspective of training a large model, how to represent an action when you need to predict it—whether actions have an optimized representation space. The FAST paper proposed that the diffusion-policy representation we had been using was one kind of representation, but that it could learn a way to represent actions. It found that, when a large model predicts in that space, it gains some performance improvements and some guarantees of generalization. This is also a very important kind of foundational research. The other paper was called Hi Robot. It considered human-robot interaction: a person may use language to get a robot to complete something, but if the robot is just one single end-to-end path, it may become lost over a 10-minute task and not know what to do now. So Hi Robot was the first to state very formally that it should be hierarchical: a higher-level policy turns the task you say into more concrete, executable, shorter subtasks. Then the lower-level execution side carries them out. They are both actually in the same model, but its outputs are hierarchically structured.

items.question: Why do you consider Physical Intelligence’s internal robot Olympics an excellent research activity?

items.answer: Looking back now, several interesting releases include Olympics. After completing them with human-operated data, we then had our large model do and learn them, and found that it successfully accomplished some actions people had previously thought would be very difficult.

items.question: Why did you initially doubt that reinforcement learning would work for natural-language generation?
items.object: Reinforcement learning for natural-language generation
items.answer: When I had just started my PhD in 2017, I briefly worked on NLP. Oh, it was funny. I thought at the time, natural-language generation does not seem very good. items.question: What made Pi more attractive to you than academia as a place to pursue pioneering robotics research?

items.answer: At the time, I would think: if a student comes and I want to let them go for it, to do relatively pioneering work, are three years enough? As you can see, I was a PhD student who came to this midway through my path. I wasn’t like many outstanding undergraduates now, who already do a great deal of related research as undergraduates; by the time they start a PhD, I think they already understand their field very well. If I were recruiting students, I would really like that kind of student, but I might also like students who dare to abandon what they did before and explore something new. And if you give them only three years, only five years even, might that not be enough time? Then a student comes, does one project, and leaves; perhaps you have only started something. I think in the current environment this model may indeed not be able to achieve what I want to do. Meanwhile, in industry there is more support in compute, data, and hardware. items.question: How do you understand reinforcement learning as a way of becoming better through experience?
items.object: Reinforcement learning as learning from experience and a path toward generality
items.answer: I think reinforcement learning is a very fundamental class of problems—namely, how a person becomes better through experience. In the most traditional textbook explanation, reinforcement learning is really explained through Pavlov’s dog. The dog does something, you give it a reward, and from then on it knows this is a good thing and I should do more of it. It is a way of using rewards and punishments to make an agent take actions that are better from your perspective. But reinforcement learning, algorithmically, I think there are things about it that, even every day, make me feel it has a great deal to do with my own evolution as a person—with human self-improvement. Whether it is a very concrete action—for example, imagine you are someone who wants to learn rock climbing or swimming—how do you get better? You keep doing it. I think pursuing the extreme is a very strong element of reinforcement learning: practicing continuously. At the same time, another important part of reinforcement learning is exploration. Exploration can be large or small. It might mean shifting this muscle very slightly to the left, and then my tennis performance becomes better—that is one kind of exploration. Or it might mean: I am working on this research now, exploring one direction for how to make this robot better, and I may change direction in the future. That is also exploration. I think it is not just about a concrete problem or scenario; it is also a path toward generality. For example, I think many people are now using reinforcement learning in large language models to help improve them. With a foundation of an LLM, you let it keep trying, observing, and receiving feedback; how to gain further improvement from that feedback is an enduring question.

items.question: Why do you regard defining the task as a foundational problem in reinforcement learning?
items.object: Defining tasks and reward functions in reinforcement learning
items.answer: Reinforcement learning has what I think is a foundational question that textbooks do not discuss much: defining the problem. In LLMs, when you want something, you generally state a prompt verbally. You could say your prompt encompasses much of what it needs to know; your prompt defines the task. In robotics, there is currently no such clear connection. Even VLA models have only made a beginning: say I want you to fold clothes, but there are thousands upon thousands of ways to fold clothes, right? How do you know what form it wants the clothes folded into? In textbooks, reinforcement learning uses a reward function to capture this. Perhaps you design the reward function so that if it really folds them as intended, it gets a high reward—a piece of meat, rewarding the dog for doing well; if it does poorly, it gets a punishment. But in practice, designing a useful reward function is very difficult. People have done much reinforcement learning in simulators, such as using reinforcement learning to play Super Mario. You have a score, right? You optimize the score; that is an existing reward function. But even then, it may—what we call—abuse the reward. It finds a bug, a Super Mario bug; after finding it, reinforcement learning exploits that bug frantically. items.question: How do you think about conveying what you want an agent to do through a reward function?
items.object: Reward functions as a way to communicate task objectives to an agent
items.answer: I think, in my view, it is not a question of writing a reward function; it is a question of conveying to the agent what you want it to do. A reward function may be more a form of expression. For example, in NLP, people previously probably explored how to write a value function: doing this is good, so a higher score; doing that is bad, so a lower score. But for a period, the most useful thing in reinforcement learning in natural language was verifiable tasks. A verifiable task can exist independently of a so-called reward function. It might ask you to write a program; if the program runs, it knows with certainty that it is good. I think communicating good versus bad does not necessarily require a reward function. items.question: How has your experience using cloud agents changed your view of the role of language in vision-language-action (VLA) robot architectures?
items.object: Language-based interaction and the role of language in VLA robot architectures
items.answer: I think this mode of interaction may work, especially after I became a heavy Cloud Code user every day. I used to be somewhat skeptical. I’m relatively introverted, so I do not like talking that much. Could there be many things for which expression without speaking is better? And even with speech, often—for example, if I want you to help tidy my kitchen—it cannot capture all of what I mean. I might mean take out the trash, close the bookcase first, or other points that language alone cannot capture. But I found these cloud agents changed my imagination of this interaction mode. items.question: How do you view the role of real-robot data alongside simulation and data collected directly with human hands in robotics research?

items.answer: I do not really know whether others have a consensus or how they think; I can only speak from the information I have encountered. items.question: How do you judge what makes good robot training data?
items.object: The quality of robot training data
items.answer: I do not think academia can resolve this very clearly; I think there are several dimensions. For example, what task does this data perform? If the task is just waving a hand in the air, that may not be very meaningful. But if it is dancing, or moving an arm in response to something, it is a more meaningful task. So I think one dimension is the task itself: folding clothes, folding boxes, or picking up a water cup are all different categories of task. At the same time, in doing a task, there is what I would call action quality. If a robot can do something like this, I feel it has completed it, taken it to the extreme—like an Olympic athlete’s performance, surpassing the limits of the human body. That is one kind of action quality. You may also collect a lower-quality trajectory: to pick up a cup, it first wobbles around and then picks it up, which may not be as good. So action quality is another dimension. I also think there is action coverage. What I just discussed was one or two individual data points; from the dataset perspective, if you collect many trajectories for picking up a water cup, how much coverage does it have? How many different scenarios does it contain, and how different are they from one another? For example, every dimension of generalization mentioned just now may be a dimension of coverage to consider when you output.

items.question: Why do you think dataset labeling and annotation are important in robotics?
items.object: Dataset labeling and annotation in robotics
items.answer: I think data provides information. How can we extract more information from a mass of data? items.question: How do you see the relationship between optimizing a robot for a specific scenario and pursuing zero-shot generalization into new environments?
items.object: The relationship between scenario-specific robotics performance and zero-shot generalization
items.answer: I think they complement one another. It is true that the focus of the two kinds of work may seem unrelated at first glance, but I think they can complement each other. In robotics research, I would put it abstractly this way: there are two major themes. One is how to make its performance truly complete; the other is how to produce something convincing in a completely new, unknown domain. This may correspond to what you just described: optimizing within a specific scenario until it is complete, and zero-shot generalization into a new environment. In practice, I often feel that if you can make something complete in one scenario, you may be able to achieve better results in more scenarios. These things all help you build a higher-quality model, and a higher-quality model does not only perform better on those two tasks; it will also perform better on many related or similar problems.

items.question: Why do you see household use as such a demanding setting for robots?

items.answer: No two people’s homes and bedrooms are exactly the same. You need very strong generalization guarantees before you can enter a new bedroom and, for example, make a bed. items.question: How do you imagine society changing if general-purpose robots and AI bring about an enormous explosion in productivity?
items.object: A productivity explosion enabled by general-purpose robots and AI
items.answer: Let's assume there is an enormous explosion in productivity in this era—then perhaps you would finally no longer have to be criticized by your visiting parents for how messy and dirty your home is. You could hand off everything you do not want to do to others, to other robots. And perhaps, for example in artistic creation now, friends make small handicrafts. I think it may become more a matter of having the concept, while you can hand all the execution-side work to robots. I think that is also one direction. Then, with a more far-reaching productivity explosion, perhaps once you have resources you could build a castle yourself and go live in seclusion somewhere in the countryside. You see some old castles being auctioned online for only tens of thousands of U.S. dollars—you can buy a castle that has not been repaired in two hundred years. No one buys it now because it is too troublesome: it needs repairs, and you need to find many specialists. I think there is an interesting characteristic: many occupations in modern society are specialized occupations. You spend a great deal of your time as a human being training a skill, and you possess a great deal of knowledge. But a robot or AI, as a large model or a general-purpose thing, can switch at any time. For example, in the future perhaps there really will be two house-repair robots. They can do everything, cooperate with each other, and eliminate the need for the different trades currently required to complete such work. Our research now may be somewhat similar. Previously, to do research you might have needed to find a specialist A responsible for something; they might have had certain insights. But now you ask the same model, and it can reach that level. So I think that in the future, if everyone has some kind of general-purpose productivity at their disposal, and every specific task is at an expert level, then we could truly reach a productivity explosion—do many things we would not even dare to imagine now, and create better games and novels.

items.question: How do you think about Silicon Valley’s tendency to optimize every step and commit early to a single competitive path?
items.object: Continuous optimization and early commitment to a single path in Silicon Valley
items.answer: When I did competitive programming as a child, I learned some algorithms. Greedy algorithms and dynamic programming are two things often compared together. A greedy algorithm means that at every point in time, I must make the optimal decision; I must do what is best in the present. Dynamic programming tells you that if you have some global perspective, you will find that making the best decision at every step cannot get you to the globally optimal solution. I really like the logic in that. So often I think it is like the saying, “A loss may be a blessing in disguise.” Temporary success or failure, optimization, or whether something has been pushed to the extreme cannot represent the final long-term outcome. Because none of us has an omnipotent, omniscient perspective, even on the path of pursuing optimization, I sometimes think it is okay to do nine out of ten and leave one part undone. My own educational journey and all kinds of other things may, in many people's eyes, look like I never take things to the end. Perhaps robots will be the first thing for which I feel that we must take it all the way to the end. But it was precisely all those earlier things I did not take to the end that led me onto the path I am on today. I think this is fundamentally somewhat different from Silicon Valley, where many people often get onto the same path very early and keep competing on it.

items.question: Why do you love Edinburgh so much?
items.object: Edinburgh
items.answer: I really love Edinburgh. During my brief half-year studying in the UK, it was probably my favorite city. Perhaps in the past, because I liked being alone, and because major cities are often actually alike, I had not so much felt that entering a completely different physical space could change my entire state so greatly. Edinburgh has a great many old buildings, and they are very well preserved. It also does not have as much of the bustle of a big city. It is even a little like a tourist city; everyone goes to see that castle. But in that city, there is a feeling of slowing down, a feeling of contemplation. History, such a weighty thing, is placed before you, and in this fleeting moment you want to make a very big, dynamic change. items.question: How did you interpret the studio name “Language Is World” when you first heard it?
items.object: The name “Language Is World” and language-based models’ understanding of reality
items.answer: “Language is world”—my instinctive interpretation was that language is the entire world. Then my thoughts jumped to: isn't this the brain-in-a-vat? We are actually living in something connected through all our senses; all your senses govern all your knowledge of this whole world. It is entirely imaginable that we live in a huge simulator: your eyes, nose, and ears are all plugged into a signal source, and that signal source can feed you whatever it wants. Because in current research—research circles—people say that large language models have purely language-based interaction. With the previous generation of purely language-based interaction, could they not understand the real world? Could they not take a concept they heard and place it in the real world? At that level, there are many physical properties they cannot capture, cannot grasp, and cannot describe in language. I think this reflection also indirectly helped bring about multimodal research.
